::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Vapour will not condense onto nothing. Clouds form on microscopic particles already floating in the air, and without them the sky would need several hundred percent humidity.
:::

## Vapour needs a surface

If the atmosphere contained only pure water vapor and nitrogen/oxygen, **clouds would almost never form**.

For pure water vapor to condense spontaneously into a spherical droplet (**homogeneous nucleation**), it must overcome the enormous surface tension barrier ($2 \sigma / r$). Droplets smaller than a few nanometers have such high vapor pressure that they evaporate instantly unless the relative humidity exceeds **$300\% - 400\%$**!

Nature solves this through **heterogeneous nucleation** using **Cloud Condensation Nuclei (CCN)**: microscopic aerosol particles ($0.1 - 2.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) such as sea salt ($\text{NaCl}$), sulfate aerosols ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$), mineral dust, and organic biogenic pollen.

## A first look at the Köhler curve

The equilibrium saturation ratio $S = e / e_s$ over an aqueous solution droplet of radius $r$ containing dissolved solute mass $m_s$ is given by **Köhler Theory**:

$$\ln(S) = \underbrace{\frac{2 \sigma_{\text{w/a}} M_w}{R T \rho_w r}}_{\text{Kelvin Effect (Curvature increases evaporation)}} - \underbrace{\frac{i \cdot \phi_s \cdot M_w \cdot m_s}{M_s \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi \rho_w r^3}}_{\text{Raoult Effect (Solute lowers vapor pressure)}}$$

When supersaturation slightly exceeds the critical threshold $S^* \approx 100.1\%$, the droplet crosses the critical radius $r^*$ and enters unstable runaway growth, ballooning into a full-sized cloud droplet ($10 - 30\text{ }\mu\text{m}$).

## Key takeaways

- Pure vapour will not condense into droplets at $100\%$ humidity; the curvature barrier means homogeneous nucleation needs $300$ to $400\%$ RH, which the atmosphere never provides.
- Clouds form by heterogeneous nucleation on cloud condensation nuclei: sea salt, sulfate, mineral dust and organic particles $0.1$ to $2\ \mu\text{m}$ across.
- The Köhler equation balances the Kelvin curvature term, which raises the equilibrium vapour pressure, against the Raoult solute term, which lowers it.
- Once ambient supersaturation exceeds the critical value, about $100.1\%$ RH, the droplet passes its critical radius and grows without limit into a $10$ to $30\ \mu\text{m}$ cloud droplet.
